# []{#anchor}Limitations

## []{#anchor-1}Temporal resolution and conservative volatility estimates

The reliance on monthly-averaged groundwater levels mathematically dampens the event-scale fluctuations inherent to highly conductive unconfined aquifers. Because daily peaks and troughs of individual storm events are smoothed over a 30-day window, the derived water balance parameters are optimized for seasonal trend analysis rather than event-based flood routing. This is a standard constraint in historic groundwater modelling (Taylor and Alley, 2001), and means the model captures the overall volumetric water balance while inherently underestimating daily transient spikes. The assessment of seasonal amplitude presented here is therefore conservative: the actual event-scale fluctuation --- and any periodic severing of the capillary fringe from the root zone --- is likely more pronounced than the monthly averages depict.

## []{#anchor-2}**Record length --- the difference between a level and a rate**

The binding constraint on this study is the length of the record rather than the density of the network, and it falls unevenly across the results. Over the full record the site-mean level moves about its own fitted trend with an interannual residual standard deviation of 286 mm on the spring basis and 213 mm on the annual basis. Against variability of that order, and over the twenty-one years available, the smallest site-wide rate of change this record could distinguish from zero at 80 % power is about ±30 mm yr⁻¹ on either basis. Every site-mean trend the record yields falls inside that threshold, and the two longest windows return opposite signs on overlapping data. Bringing the threshold down to the order of 7 mm yr⁻¹ would take a record of roughly five decades at the present variability.

The consequence is a division by estimator rather than by importance, and it is set out in full in Section 5.7.7. A quantity estimated as a difference between groups, or as a contrast across space at one time, is not exposed to interannual variability in the same way, because the variability is common to both sides of the contrast and cancels; a quantity estimated as a rate through time from the site mean has no such protection. The clearfell step, the scraping steps, the coastal gradient and the epoch contrast against the 1989--96 record are of the first kind and are resolved. The secular trend, the far-field constant and the post-felling trajectory are of the second kind and are not. Where a rate would have to be obtained by dividing a resolved contrast by an interval containing no observations --- as it would for the 1989--96 comparison --- the division is not performed and no rate is quoted. Readers should treat every level and every contrast in this work as supported by the record, and treat the absence of quoted site-wide rates as deliberate.

## []{#anchor-3}**Parallel trends --- unverifiable rather than violated**

The difference-in-differences design underlying the BACI analyses assumes that, absent the intervention, the felled and control wells would have continued to diverge at whatever rate they diverged at beforehand. That assumption is conventionally supported by demonstrating that the pre-intervention trends were parallel. At this record length it cannot be supported in either direction. The pre-felling comparison is a rate estimated over a window of a few years from a quantity with the variability described above, and it sits far below the detection threshold: the pre-felling trends are neither demonstrably parallel nor demonstrably divergent, and the test has no power to distinguish the two. This is a limitation of the record, not a finding about the design, and it should not be read as a violated assumption.

The step estimates are reported accordingly. Each is a discontinuity at the intervention date, net of a linear drift control between treatment and control wells, which is the conservative construction because it charges any accumulating divergence to the control rather than to the intervention. Their support comes from agreement across methods that rest on different assumptions --- the ANCOVA, synthetic control and SSM residual normalization, which return steps in the same direction and at comparable magnitude --- rather than from a verified parallel-trends premise. A longer pre-intervention baseline is the only thing that would convert the assumption from untestable to tested, and the requirement is taken up with the other record-length constraints in Section 5.9.

## []{#anchor-3}**Thornthwaite PET and sensitivity of absolute thresholds**

The Thornthwaite method was selected for its compatibility with the low-cost replication objective (Section 3.10), and its systematic biases cancel in all cluster-to-cluster and before-versus-after comparisons because the same PET series is applied uniformly across all clusters and time periods (Section 3.1.2). However, the absolute values produced by the prediction equations and P_flood thresholds are sensitive to the PET input. Thornthwaite PET overestimates evaporative demand by approximately 10--15% relative to Penman-Monteith in humid maritime climates (Donohue et al., 2010). Because the SSM\'s atmospheric draw term is β₂ × PET, a 15% reduction in PET would reduce the fitted β₂ coefficients proportionally, with the effect concentrated in the summer months when PET is largest. The P_flood threshold --- which depends on the winter recharge demand required to offset the preceding summer\'s atmospheric losses --- would decrease, meaning the critical rainfall target would be easier to achieve than the current equations suggest. The scenario framework Δh estimates would be similarly affected: the absolute magnitude of forest management responses would be smaller if PET were lower, because the canopy interception and atmospheric draw perturbations are scaled against the PET baseline. The relative ranking of scenarios, the spatial pattern of responses, and the finding that forest management perturbations do not propagate to C1/C2 are all independent of the PET method because they depend on coefficient ratios and spatial structure rather than absolute magnitudes. Users of the P_flood equations and scenario framework should therefore treat the absolute thresholds as conservative upper bounds on rainfall demand, consistent with the upper-bound interpretation applied to the WTF-derived specific yield estimates (Section 4.2.4).

The bias is not only in level but in response. Thornthwaite carries the heat index I in its denominator and builds I from the same monthly temperatures, so a warming climate raises numerator and denominator together and the formula partly cancels its own response. Over the RAF Valley record, mean annual temperature rose 0.73 °C between the first and last thirty complete years (1931--1960 against 1996--2025), a rise of 7.2%, while mean annual Thornthwaite PET rose only 3.0%, from 631 to 650 mm --- an elasticity of 0.42. The PET series the models are fitted to therefore carries roughly two-fifths of the warming signal the temperature record shows. This does not affect the cluster-to-cluster and before-versus-after comparisons discussed above, in which the same series is applied throughout. It does mean that where a result is interpreted as a response to rising evaporative demand, the demand implied by the temperature record is larger than the forcing the model was given, so the atmospheric-draw route is understated rather than overstated.

## []{#anchor-4}The NW10 broadleaf comparison --- a single uncontrolled well

The comparison of NW10 (broadleaf block, established 1993--1996) with adjacent Corsican pine wells represents the only direct observational evidence of species conversion effects within the monitoring network, but it is subject to several limitations that preclude a fully controlled comparison. NW10 is a single well in a single block; replication across multiple broadleaf wells and blocks would be required to establish a statistically robust species effect independent of local variation. The comparison wells (CEH2, CEH34) differ from NW10 in ground elevation, distance from the ridge, and drainage rate (NW10 β₃ = 0.043 vs C4 median 0.019), and whilst the direction of the summer minimum contrast is consistent across all comparators the absolute magnitude is sensitive to these positional differences. Most significantly, the broadleaf stand was characterized by a dense bramble understorey throughout most of the monitoring period, which maintained high ground-level evapotranspiration demand and confounded the tree canopy signal. The stand has only begun to approach a closed canopy configuration from approximately 2022, leaving fewer than four years of post-closure record. The conclusions drawn from NW10 should therefore be treated as indicative observations from a natural experiment rather than confirmed causal attributions, and will require validation against a longer post-closure record and, ideally, against additional broadleaf wells installed within the block.

## []{#anchor-5}Spatial analysis --- absence of calibrated continuous-flow modelling

The spatial framework used in this study (Sections 3.8, 4.9) is a per-well SSM scenario aggregator interpolated by inverse-distance weighting, not a calibrated continuous-flow model. It is well-suited to the questions the paper addresses --- how the per-well β parameterization aggregates spatially under scenarios, and whether the BACI-observed forest response propagates beyond the forest zone --- but cannot represent cluster-to-cluster hydraulic coupling or the diffusive redistribution of localized recharge perturbations. Hydraulic conductivity is constrained by a single tracer test (K = 6.0 m/day; Betson et al., 2002) and aquifer thickness in the western interior is inferred from four borehole logs across 700 ha (Bristow, 2003). These are the same parameter-sparsity constraints that produced calibration difficulties in the Betson et al. (2002) MODFLOW model at this site. The priority field measurements required to enable a calibrated continuous-flow model are identified in Section 5.9.

## []{#anchor-6}BACI experiment --- network design limitations

The clearfell zone and scraping sites were selected on different grounds: scraping was a targeted conservation intervention, while the clearfell was an experimental felling recommended by previous researchers and implemented as an operational forestry action. Neither was randomly assigned, which introduces the possibility that pre-existing site characteristics could confound the intervention signal. The monitoring network was not designed as a purpose-built propagation transect. The transect analysis in Section 4.6.7 (Figure 36) uses the available surveillance wells to test for an inland gradient in the post-felling signal and finds none, with post-felling step changes distributed uniformly from the plantation interior to the felling core. All 17 wells in the five-tier network have a minimum of eight years\' pre-felling baseline (Section 3.5.4). Wells with shorter records (FE1--4, LIS1, NW8B) were excluded from the analysis. The network permits a test of whether clearfell-driven effects propagate into the adjacent warren, but does not provide fine-grained spatial resolution of any residual propagation signal at distances under 100 m from the clearfell edge, nor a purpose-built warren transect perpendicular to the clearfell boundary.

## []{#anchor-7}Coastal-erosion confound --- first-order spatial control rather than time-lagged propagation

Both intervention analyses treat the coastal-erosion confound through covariates and control selection rather than through explicit time-lagged modelling. The clearfell ANCOVA includes an Easting × time interaction that captures average differential deterioration with proximity to the coast across the observation window, and the scraping analysis tracks coastal-driven drift through CEH4\'s CUSUM trajectory and through the synthetic-control and SSM-forward-residual robustness checks. Neither approach explicitly represents the multi-year to multi-decadal propagation timescale (L²Sy/K, Section 5.4.3) over which coastal erosion signals travel inland through the aquifer. The result is that both intervention analyses estimate the felling-attributable and scraping-attributable steps cleanly within the available analysis windows, but cannot fully separate the contemporaneous management signal from the time-integrated coastal-erosion signal arriving from earlier historical retreat.

A direct test of the spatial component of this confound is provided by the network-scale gradient regression of Section 4.10.2, which fits the strip-aquifer reach and coast-edge deepening rate directly to the 21-year monthly panel. An earlier version of this section additionally offered the clearfell ANCOVA\'s easting × time covariate as corroboration of that model; the comparison is withdrawn (Section 5.7.7), because in the paired implementation the covariate is a single scalar multiplied by elapsed months and its coefficient cannot be read as a measurement of anything spatial. The covariate remains in the ANCOVA as a control for linear divergence between treatment and control wells, which is its legitimate role, and the clearfell results do not depend on the withdrawn reading. The remaining limitation is the absence of an explicit transient boundary-condition flow model, which would refine the time-lagged propagation estimates and resolve the residual covariate absorption beyond what the steady-state gradient model captures. Direct measurement of present-day coastal retreat rates at the south-western dune front remains a monitoring priority

## []{#anchor-8}****Water balance closure as weak validation****

****The cluster-level water balance closes to within 2.5% of total losses at all five clusters (Table 4a), and the residual field is spatially uniform in magnitude, with 64 of the 66 reference wells within ±0.01 m/month and no gradient in residual magnitude across the site (Section 4.9.6). Closure of this quality is a necessary condition for the model to be trusted, but it is a weak one.****

The residual is a single scalar per well formed from the long-term means of all three fitted terms, so compensating errors cancel within it: a β₁ biased high and a β₂ biased high in the same proportion close the balance as well as two correct coefficients. Good closure at the long-term mean therefore constrains the terms jointly and says little about any one of them individually, and nothing about month-to-month adequacy, which is addressed separately by the fit statistics and the residual diagnostics of Supplementary Notes S5 and S6. The residual also absorbs nonlinear soil-moisture storage dynamics, coefficient sensitivity and any systematic bias in the Thornthwaite PET estimate indistinguishably, so a small residual cannot be read as evidence that none of these is present.

Interpretation of the field is correspondingly limited. It supports the statement that no large unmodelled flux is required anywhere in the network; it does not support inferences about the magnitude of any individual term, and management conclusions drawn in Section 5 do not rest on it.

## []{#anchor-9}**Topographic proxies, aeolian deflation, and bedrock causation**

****The strong spatial correlation between DEM-derived drainage pathways and the hydrogeological cluster boundaries confirms that surface topography acts as a reliable operational proxy for subsurface flow divides. However, this correlation does not imply direct causation: surface sand deposition patterns do not dictate groundwater divides. Both are co-determined by the underlying architecture of glacial till and bedrock ridges, where present. In coastal dune systems this structural relationship is mediated by aeolian deflation --- wind erosion is physically limited by the capillary fringe, as cohesive damp sand resists aeolian transport (Bristow and Bailey, 2001; Hesp and Thom, 1990), and because the regional water table is governed by subsurface geology, that geology indirectly controls the baseline limits of surface erosion (Haitjema and Mitchell-Bruker, 2005). Surface topography at Newborough Warren is therefore a physical expression of subsurface hydrological structure, supporting the use of the DEM as a proxy for regional groundwater routing in the absence of high-resolution bedrock mapping.****

## **MSL5 metric: application beyond its intended domain**

The five-year mean spring water level (MSL5; van Willegen et al. 2025) was validated as an ecohydrological descriptor for dune-slack vegetation communities at lake-edge, open-dune and western-residual wells (C1, C2 and C3). Its use in Section 4.12 as a network-wide change-detection tool across all clusters reflects a deliberate methodological choice: shorter comparison windows, one to three years either side of each intervention, proved too unstable to yield interpretable results because the expected management signal is smaller than the interannual variability of spring water levels at this site. Following involvement in the van Willegen et al. (2025) research on the same network, MSL5 was recognized as the most stable available metric for a longer-window empirical comparison. The spring season was selected because it is the only season in which readings are reliably obtainable across the full network: summer levels frequently fall below dipwell reach at the deeper wells, and winter readings are subject to surface ponding that truncates the measurable maximum.

Because this extends the metric beyond its original design, the properties governing its window sensitivity were characterized directly (Section 4.12). Two findings bear on its use elsewhere. First, the assumption of independence between spring readings holds: the expectation that slow-draining wells would carry a head anomaly from one spring to the next is not borne out, because spring is the seasonal maximum and each winter\'s recharge resets the water table. Second, window sensitivity is nonetheless graded across the network, but it is driven by the amplitude of interannual variation rather than by drainage memory, and that amplitude tracks the atmospheric-draw coefficient β₂ rather than the drainage coefficient β₃. Researchers applying the metric at sites with heterogeneous aquifer properties should therefore triage wells on the interannual standard deviation of spring level, or on β₂ as its structural proxy, and not on the recession time; the standard deviation has the further advantage of requiring no state-space fit. The equilibrium wetness index of Section 4.8.4 is not a substitute for change detection, being a steady-state descriptor with no before and after, and it is in any case the less precise of the two indices at every cluster.

The check that remains generally applicable is the external one. Testing whether the chosen window\'s spatial pattern correlates with an independent long-run trend metric, such as the per-well summer-minimum slope, distinguishes a genuine secular signal from a window-specific artefact; at this site the 2017→2023 window converges with that metric at r = 0.47 (Section 5.7.5). A worked illustration of why the internal checks require care is provided by the anomalously wet 2024 spring. Excluding it from the window ending 2025 reduces the apparent Forest Control gain from +127 mm to +24 mm, which invites the conclusion that the gain was an artefact specific to those wells; but the open-dune Climate Control gain falls further over the same operation, and the excess between the two groups moves only from +90 mm to +76 mm. Removing an anomalous spring changes both the signal and its comparator, and does not by itself isolate a cluster-specific effect.
